summary: This work uses scanning SQUID susceptometry to spatially image the diamagnetic response in S-S'-S transition edge sensors, directly resolving proximity effects that extend over tens of micrometers and reveal how neighboring superconducting leads enhance while normal metal contacts suppress the local transition temperature. Ginzburg-Landau and self-consistent Usadel modeling quantitatively capture the observed spatial structure of the superconducting state, establishing a framework for understanding proximity-induced tuning of superconducting properties in heterogeneous device geometries.
motivation: Proximity effects at superconductor interfaces govern TES performance, but spatially resolved measurements within functional devices have been lacking; direct imaging of how geometry controls the local superconducting state is essential for detector engineering and understanding weak-link behavior in S-S'-S structures.
method: Scanning SQUID with concentric field and pickup coils measured local diamagnetic response $\delta M(T)$ across functional AlMn/Nb and MoAu/Mo TES devices; extracted spatially varying local critical temperatures $T_c^\chi$ from threshold detection in image series; modeled using 1D/2D Usadel equations to calculate temperature-dependent gaps and 2D Ginzburg-Landau equations to map order parameter spatial structure.
result: Proximity coupling from Nb leads shifted transition temperatures by $\sim10$ mK in AlMn and enhanced $T_c^\chi$ above $T_c^0=92.8$ mK in MoAu devices over $\sim5$–$10$ µm; inverse proximity from Au banks suppressed $T_c^\chi$ along edges; in the 100 µm meander geometry, weakly superconducting MoAu bilayer proximitized 10 µm wide normal Au fingers at low temperature, demonstrating long-range Cooper-pair penetration depth effects.
